title: Reviewing a pull request in the order it runs
excerpt: GitHub lists a pull request's files by path. grain groups the changes into blocks, then walks the call graph from every page and screen, so you review the code a user hits together, in the order it runs. No AI decides the order: the same commit always gives the same review.
contentHtml:
dub's pull request #4697 adds an Earnings page. It changes 28 files. GitHub shows them by path, so the new page.tsx comes first and the chart it renders, the biggest change in the PR at 278 changed lines, comes 23rd. To review the page, you read file 1, skip 21 files to reach the chart, then go back to file 18 for the data hook and on to 26 for the chart's filters.

grain is a review tool I built to fix that. It reads a PR as a story: for each page or screen, the changed code that runs there, in the order it runs. Code that nothing reaches comes after, and lockfiles and generated files come last. On that PR it turns 28 files into 6 blocks in 3 chapters, and the Earnings page reads top to bottom: the page, the hook it calls, the chart, the chart's filters.

Nothing in that order comes from an AI model. Grouping is plain code over a parse tree and a call graph, and opening the same commit twice gives exactly the same review. This post is about how it gets there.

From lines to functions

A diff knows lines and files. A reviewer thinks in functions and components. So the first step is to find which function each changed line belongs to.

grain runs git diff -U0 -M for the changed line numbers, then uses sem-core, a Rust library that parses source with tree-sitter and lists its functions, classes and methods across 28 languages. Each changed line is assigned to the innermost entity that contains it. Lines outside any entity, like imports and top-level config, become one leftover unit per file.

Most code lives in entities, so this loses very little. On four internal PRs I measured before building anything, from 22 to 2,648 files, between 97.4% and 98.7% of changed lines landed inside an entity. Parsing is cheap: the semantic diff took 36 ms on a 22-file PR and 427 ms on a 2,648-file release merge.

The grouping that didn't work

My first grouping was the obvious one: if changed function A calls changed function B, they belong together. Union-find over call edges, done.

It failed in both directions at once. Every codebase has hubs: a logger, a theme, an API client, a useTranslation. A hub that's touched in a PR links everything that calls it, so 70 to 80% of a PR chained into one giant block. Changes that called nothing else stayed alone, as dozens of one-to-five-line blocks. You got one block you couldn't review and forty you didn't need to.

Blocks that fit in your head

The version that works groups files, not functions, and caps what it builds:

  • Repeated edits become one block. If three or more files in the same folder carry nearly the same edit (13 locale files, a codemod across components), grain compares the shapes of the edited lines with string literals and numbers stripped out. Files whose shapes overlap by 70% or more (Jaccard similarity) are reviewed as one block: read one, skim the rest.
  • Lockfiles, generated files and assets each get one block per kind and stay out of the rest of the grouping.
  • Everything else is merged by weight. Each call between changed entities in two files adds 1 to the link between those files. A test and the file it tests (same name stem) add 5. Links are merged heaviest first, and a merge only happens if the result stays under 400 changed lines.
  • Small leftovers are absorbed. A block under 60 lines joins its strongest neighbour, else a sibling in the same folder.

Most blocks come out between 50 and 400 lines, and components land in the same block as their tests. The 400-line cap is the important part: no amount of linking can rebuild the one giant block.

Finding the screens

Blocks alone are a better list. The story needs one more thing: who runs this code?

A user doesn't call functions; they open a page. So grain finds the files a user can open, by the conventions frameworks already use:

pub(crate) fn is_entry_file(path: &str) -> bool {
    let l = format!("/{}", path.to_lowercase());
    let name = l.rsplit('/').next().unwrap_or("");
    let stem = name.split('.').next().unwrap_or("");
    let js = [".ts", ".tsx", ".js", ".jsx", ".mjs"].iter().any(|e| name.ends_with(e));
    if !js || is_test_path(&l) || l.contains("/mocks/") || l.contains("/__mocks__/") {
        return false;
    }
    // Screens folders also hold hooks and helpers; only components (JSX files, not `use…`) are screens.
    let component = (name.ends_with(".tsx") || name.ends_with(".jsx")) && !stem.starts_with("use");
    (l.contains("/app/") && matches!(stem, "page" | "route"))
        || l.contains("/pages/")
        || (l.contains("/screens/") && component)
        || (stem.ends_with("screen") && component)
}

That covers the Next.js app and pages routers and React Native screens. Navigators, routers, layouts and _app also match, but they reach almost everything, so grain marks them as weak entries. Storybook, preview and debug pages get a chapter of their own.

From every top-level function in every entry file, grain walks the call graph breadth-first, up to 14 calls deep, and records each changed block it reaches and how many calls away it is. The call graph comes from sem-core, with one addition: it doesn't record JSX, and in a React codebase <EarningsCompositeChart /> is the most important call there is. So grain scans .tsx and .jsx files for capitalised tags and resolves each one through the file's imports to the component's definition.

One block, one chapter

A shared component is reachable from many screens. If it appeared in every flow that reaches it, you'd review it five times. So each block goes to exactly one flow, chosen by a sort key:

let key = (is_weak_entry(file), h.depth, hits.len(), fi);

Read left to right: a real page beats a layout; then the fewest calls away wins; then the flow that reaches fewer changed blocks, which is the more specific screen; then the entry's position in path order, so a tie can never be decided by chance.

Inside a flow, blocks are ordered by call depth, so you read the page, then what it renders, then what that uses. Flows under 300 changed lines share an "Other screens" chapter with one section per route, which is where four of the dub flows went. Flows over 1,200 lines are split by component: grain walks down the call path while one child holds every change, then splits by child, into at most seven sections. Blocks no flow reaches go in "Also changed", grouped by feature folder with the riskiest first. Routine changes end the story.

Same commit, same review

The first version of this engine wasn't deterministic. Ties in merge weights, in neighbour choice and in block order were broken by Rust's HashMap iteration order, which is randomised per process, so the same PR could come out as different blocks on two runs.

The fix was one rule, now written into the architecture notes: never let hash-map iteration order decide anything, and give every sort a full tie-break. It's why the sort key above ends in a file index. A reviewer who reopens a PR tomorrow, or a colleague opening it on another machine, sees the same chapters in the same order.

It's also why there's no model in the grouping. An AI summary per block is available if you turn it on, from your own coding agent's CLI (Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode), and the agent never marks or posts anything. But it explains blocks; it never decides them.

Opening big PRs fast

A tool that reorders PRs is only useful if opening one is quicker than skimming GitHub. The slow part is not the engine, which takes under a second on normal PRs and about 5 seconds on a 400,000-line release merge. It's git.

So grain opens in two stages. The first downloads and checks out only the changed files, in a sparse worktree from a partial clone, and runs the engine without the whole-repo graph. You can start reading. The second expands the checkout in the background and adds the facts that need the whole repo, like the flows and outside callers, then swaps the review in. Blocks come out identical at both stages, so what you've already read stays put; only the chapters around them change when the flows arrive. On a 2,648-file PR the checkout went from 46 s to 1.7 s, and moving to the next block takes about 50 ms because it's prefetched.

Limits

Flows only exist where grain can find pages and screens: Next.js and React Native file conventions today. Any other codebase still gets blocks, ordered in chapters by feature folder, which is better than a path-sorted list but isn't a story.

JSX resolution reads the source text. A component passed around as a value, or rendered through a registry, has no <Tag> for grain to follow, and the block it lives in will show up under "Also changed" instead of in its screen.

Precise "used by" facts come from the TypeScript language server, so other languages get grain's own graph only.

What I'd tell you to steal

Group by who runs the code, not where it lives. File paths say who wrote it. Entry points say who'll notice when it breaks, and that's the question a reviewer is answering.

Cap your clusters. Any grouping based on links will find a hub that links everything. A size cap that no merge may exceed fixes that better than any clever weighting.

Give each item one home. Assigning each block to its nearest entry, with a fixed tie-break order, turned five copies of a shared component into one, in the flow where it matters most.

Make the order deterministic, then test it. Sort with full tie-breaks and never iterate a hash map into output. If two runs can disagree, a reviewer will eventually find out and stop trusting the order.

Make the first screen fast and the rest correct. A sparse checkout and a cheaper first pass took a huge PR's checkout from 46 seconds to under 2, with the full analysis landing in the background.

grain is open source on GitHub (pranav2012/grain). Install it with brew install pranav2012/tap/grain or npm i -g grain-ci, then run grain owner/repo#123 on any PR you can see with your gh login.

title: Most of my homelab is asleep, on purpose
excerpt: Sixteen Docker Compose projects on one gaming laptop with 14 GiB of RAM. A small Python gateway starts each service when its hostname is requested and stops it after 30 idle minutes. Here's how it works and what broke.
contentHtml:
Between midnight and 2 a.m. one night this week, Uptime Kuma sent 2,036 requests to my homelab. Nobody else sent more than 120. If every one of those health checks had counted as "someone is using this", nothing on the machine would ever get to sleep, and the machine is a gaming laptop with 14 GiB of RAM running sixteen Docker Compose projects.

This post is about the setup that makes that fit. Most services are stopped most of the time. A small gateway I call WakeGate starts them when their hostname is requested and stops them after 30 minutes without real traffic. Everything else here is either there to support that or is a thing that broke because of it.

The machine and the constraints

Hardware

Acer Nitro AN515-45: Ryzen 5 5600H (6c/12t), GTX 1650 with 4 GB

Memory

~14 GiB usable, plus 8 GiB zram swap (zstd)

Storage

256 GB NVMe, Btrfs with subvolumes for /, /home, the pacman cache and /var/log; 1 TB HDD, ext4, for bulk data and backups

OS

Arch Linux

Workload

16 Compose projects, 58 containers, 32 of them running when I wrote this

The binding constraint is memory. Disk is a close second, and it keeps coming back.

One folder per stack

Every app lives in its own folder in my home directory with one docker-compose.yml: gitea/, immich/, monitoring/, registry/, zerobyte/, and so on. Shared infrastructure (Traefik, the Cloudflare connector, a Docker UI, WakeGate's config) sits in management-stack/.

Two habits make this layout pay off. First, nearly every container gets a mem_limit (Honcho is the exception I still owe a fix): 192m for Traefik, 512m for Prometheus, 1024m for Gitea. A memory leak then takes out one container, not the box. Second, a user systemd timer compares every compose file with its copy in a Gitea repo every 15 minutes and commits whatever changed, so the infrastructure has history even when I edit it in place at 1 a.m. That timer comes back later as a bug.

The daily updater finds stacks by looking for compose files, so adding a stack is just adding a folder.

Private by default

Nothing on the laptop accepts connections from the internet. There are two ways in.

The private path is Tailscale. Traefik's ports are bound to the laptop's tailnet address only, so they're unreachable from my home LAN, let alone the internet. Each service still gets a real hostname and a real certificate. A sync script writes a DNS-only A record per service that points at the tailnet address, and Traefik gets Let's Encrypt certificates through the DNS-01 challenge, which never needs an inbound connection. Off the tailnet, those hostnames resolve to an address you can't route to.

The public path is a Cloudflare Tunnel. cloudflared dials out to Cloudflare and forwards requests to a separate Traefik entrypoint. Only routers attached to that entrypoint are public, so making something public means changing its entrypoint, not opening a port. Today exactly one app is routed that way: the CMS behind my portfolio, which has its own login. I like this split because the default is safe: a new service I forget to think about ends up private.

WakeGate: scale to zero for Docker Compose

WakeGate is about 380 lines of Python with aiohttp, running as a user systemd service. Traefik terminates TLS and forwards every service's hostname to WakeGate. WakeGate looks up the Host header in a YAML file to find which containers that hostname needs.

default_idle_timeout_seconds: 1800
health_interval_seconds: 2
ignored_access_user_agents:
  - uptime-kuma

services:
  - name: immich
    hosts: [immich.<domain>]
    target: http://<tailnet-address>:<port>
    start: wakegate-start immich_postgres immich_redis immich_machine_learning immich_server
    stop: docker stop immich_server immich_machine_learning immich_redis immich_postgres
    startup_timeout_seconds: 300

The start and stop fields are shell commands, so a service doesn't have to be a container. My agent dashboard and code-server are user systemd units, and the same file wakes them with systemctl --user start.

Intercept, wake, proxy

Every request goes through one handler. This is the real code, trimmed:

async def handle(self, request):
    svc = self.service_for_request(request)          # Host header -> service
    user_agent = request.headers.get("User-Agent", "").lower()
    synthetic = any(m in user_agent for m in self.ignored_access_user_agents)
    if not synthetic:
        self.touch(svc)                               # reset the group's idle clock

    if not await self.group_is_healthy(svc):
        if synthetic:
            return web.Response(status=204, text="")  # monitors never wake anything
        if any(request.path.startswith(p) for p in svc.wait_for_backend_paths):
            await self.ensure_started(svc)            # API clients wait for the real answer
            return await self.proxy_http(request, svc)
        if svc.starting is None or svc.starting.done():
            svc.starting = asyncio.create_task(self.ensure_started(svc))
        if "text/html" in request.headers.get("Accept", "") or request.method == "GET":
            return self.loader(request, svc)          # 202 + a page that refreshes every 3 s
        return web.Response(status=503, headers={"Retry-After": "3"})

    return await self.proxy_http(request, svc)

A browser that hits a sleeping service gets a small "waking up" page with a meta refresh. Once the health checks pass, the next refresh lands on the real app. Native clients can't do anything with an HTML page, so a few path prefixes (/api/, /oauth/) hold the request open until the backend is up and then proxy the real response.

ensure_started is where groups matter. A hostname is healthy only when every member of its group answers, and the group lock makes sure ten parallel requests produce one start command, not ten:

async def ensure_started(self, svc):
    if await self.group_is_healthy(svc):
        return
    async with self.group_locks[self.group_name(svc)]:
        if await self.group_is_healthy(svc):   # someone else started it while we waited
            return
        if svc.start:
            rc, out = await self.run_shell(svc.start, timeout=120)
            if rc != 0:
                raise web.HTTPServiceUnavailable(text=f"Failed to start: {out}\n")
        deadline = time.time() + svc.startup_timeout_seconds
        while time.time() < deadline:
            if await self.group_is_healthy(svc):
                return
            await asyncio.sleep(self.health_interval_seconds)
        raise web.HTTPServiceUnavailable(text="Timed out waiting for group\n")

"Healthy" is deliberately loose: any HTTP status from 200 to 499 counts. A login redirect or a 401 still proves the process is up and serving.

Idling out

A background loop runs every 60 seconds. For each group, it checks that the stop is allowed, that no WebSockets are open, and that the last real request was at least idle_timeout_seconds ago. Then it runs the group's stop command. A stop sets a stopping flag under the same lock that new WebSocket connections take. A socket that arrives mid-teardown waits for the stop to finish, then wakes a clean backend. That race was a real bug with a long-lived editor connection.

Setting stop_when_idle: false keeps a service on but still routed through WakeGate. That's the always-on core: Traefik, the tunnel, DNS, monitoring, the registry, the portfolio CMS, and an AI proxy that a Slack bot calls directly.

In the week before I wrote this, the journal shows 48 idle stops. Cold starts, measured from the start command to "group is healthy":

Group

Containers

Cold start

Admin dashboard

1

2 s

Agent dashboard (systemd unit)

1

4–7 s

Honcho (memory service)

5

7–20 s

Firecrawl

5

30–32 s

For things I open a few times a day, a few seconds of loader page is a fine trade for the memory back.

Making docker start reliable

docker start fails in ways Compose doesn't. A stopped container can hold a reference to a network that has since been deleted, or Docker can believe an old endpoint is still attached. So the start command is a small wrapper, wakegate-start. It skips containers that are already running, tries docker start, and if that fails, reads the container's own Compose labels to find its project and recreates just that service:

labels = payload.get("Config", {}).get("Labels", {}) or {}
service = labels.get("com.docker.compose.service")
files = [p for p in labels.get("com.docker.compose.project.config_files", "").split(",") if p]
command = ["docker", "compose"]
for path in files:
    command.extend(["-f", path])
command.extend(["up", "-d", "--no-deps", "--force-recreate", service])

Note the split(","). Compose stores multiple config files as one comma-joined label, and my updater once treated that string as a single path. The management stack failed to reconcile until I fixed it.

What it costs

This is a single docker stats --no-stream snapshot, not an average. At that moment the always-on containers added up to about 1.24 GiB. The on-demand stacks that happened to be awake used about 4.1 GiB, and nearly three quarters of that was Firecrawl. I had woken it 16 minutes earlier, and it would stop on its own 30 minutes after its last request. The host as a whole showed 10 GiB of 14 GiB used, with 2.3 GiB of data sitting in zram compressed to 693 MiB.

The biggest bar on the chart is the one that leaves on its own. That's the point of the design. If Immich, Nextcloud, Jellyfin, Stirling PDF and the rest were also resident, their mem_limits alone would add several GiB more.

Shipping my own apps

My own software goes through the same box. Gitea hosts the repos, and a registry:3 container serves images over the tailnet. Builds aren't automated yet: I (or my assistant) run docker build on the laptop, tag the image with the short commit hash, and push it. Honcho runs as honcho:1ae72b1. A deploy is a commit to the compose file that bumps the tag, like deploy: run the CMS image 4a9e82d in the portfolio repo. A commit tag tells me what's running from docker ps alone, and rolling back means putting the previous tag back. I haven't actually had to roll back yet. Third-party stacks still float on latest and get pulled by a daily updater. That's a known gap.

The portfolio CMS is a good example of the shape. It's Payload CMS in a container on the laptop. The public site is static and built by Cloudflare from GitHub, so it never talks to the CMS. When I save in the CMS, a publish script exports the content as JSON into a checkout of the site repo and pushes it. The push is the deploy. The part I'd reuse is the retry loop, because two saves in a row race each other:

for attempt in 1 2 3; do
    git_ fetch --quiet --depth 1 origin "$BRANCH"
    git reset --quiet --hard "origin/$BRANCH"
    node "$EXPORT" "$DIR/web/src/content"
    git add -A web/src/content web/public
    if git diff --cached --quiet; then
        echo "Content unchanged; nothing to publish"; exit 0
    fi
    git commit --quiet -m "content: update from the CMS"
    if git_ push --quiet origin "HEAD:$BRANCH"; then exit 0; fi
    echo "Push rejected because $BRANCH moved; trying again (attempt $attempt)"
done

The token goes in through an http.extraHeader, so it's never written into the checkout's git config.

Backups that actually back up

ZeroByte runs backups at 01:00 to a repository on the HDD and at 02:00 to Google Drive. It's also an on-demand service, which creates an obvious problem: a backup scheduler that's been asleep for 30 minutes doesn't run its schedule. Two timers handle it. One curls ZeroByte's hostname through WakeGate every 20 minutes from 00:00 to 02:40, so the service wakes and stays awake. The other stops it at 03:05.

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/bin/curl -fsS -H "Host: <zerobyte-host>" http://<wakegate-address>/

In July I noticed the backup-complete notifications had stopped. The timers were firing. The last successful local and Drive backups were from June 24. The container had exited and couldn't start: failed to set up container networking: network … not found. It still referenced a Docker network that no longer existed. Recreating only that container (docker compose up -d --force-recreate --no-deps zerobyte) created a fresh network and kept all 11 of its mounts. wakegate-start now tries that same recreate on its own when docker start fails.

The lesson I took is about the keepalive, not Docker. curl -f only fails on 4xx and 5xx responses. WakeGate answers a sleeping service with a 202 loader page and starts it in the background, so the keepalive "succeeded" every 20 minutes for weeks while the start failed behind it. Whatever reports success has to check the thing you care about. Here that's a completed snapshot, not an HTTP status. I still haven't run a full restore test.

Other things that broke

Twelve quiet days

The same blind spot came back in October. Home Assistant couldn't start from at least October 2 to October 14, and Gitea's Postgres from October 7. Docker thought their old network endpoints still existed: endpoint with name homeassistant already exists in network host. WakeGate logged 5,006 of those failures. The recreate fallback couldn't help. Home Assistant isn't a Compose container, and Postgres hit the same error after it was recreated. It cleared on October 14, after a Docker upgrade and a full reboot. I don't know what created the stale endpoints in the first place.

Monitoring couldn't have caught it. A monitor request to a sleeping service gets a 204, and Uptime Kuma counts a 204 as up. Exempting monitors from waking things also made them blind to "can't wake".

The Gitea failures also showed me why Gitea kept waking in the first place. The compose sync runs every 15 minutes, which is shorter than the 30-minute idle timeout, so Gitea is effectively always on. That's true even though every run that day found nothing to change. Any job that runs more often than the idle timeout keeps its target awake.

zram wants MiB

My first /etc/systemd/zram-generator.conf said zram-size = 8G. zram-generator reads that field as an expression in MiB, not a size with a suffix. Setup failed with Cannot allocate memory (os error 12), and the kernel logged a vmalloc request of 32,768,000,000,000 bytes. 6G failed the same way. zram-size = 8192 works.

Traefik and multiple networks

A Slack webhook receiver sat on three Docker networks. Traefik's Docker provider picked an address on one it couldn't reach, so requests hung until curl gave up after 5 seconds. The fix was one label, traefik.docker.network=management-stack_default. The same request then returned the expected 401.

Images filling the disk

In August a docker image prune -f reclaimed 12.63 GB, and image storage dropped from 88.59 GB to 75.97 GB. A prune now runs after every update. It doesn't touch the build cache, though, and when I last checked, docker system df reported 27.32 GB of it on a 256 GB drive. Build cache needs its own prune.

Local models that never leave

Honcho, a memory service my assistant uses, calls a small local model through Ollama for background work. Ollama was configured with OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=15m, and Honcho's background jobs could keep refreshing that timer, so the models stayed resident in RAM and VRAM while nothing interactive was happening. The embedding model alone sat at 323 MB on the GPU. WakeGate can stop Honcho's containers, but Ollama runs on the host and keeps its own idle timer. Scale-to-zero has to cover every layer that holds memory, or it doesn't cover any. That one is still open.

What I'd tell you to steal

  1. Put the wake logic in the proxy. You don't need Kubernetes for scale-to-zero. You need something on the request path that maps a hostname to a start command, a health check and a last-seen timestamp. Group the containers that have to start together, and serve browsers a page that refreshes itself while API clients wait.
  2. Decide which traffic counts as use. Monitors, sync jobs and keepalives all send requests. Ignore the ones that shouldn't keep a service awake, and compare every periodic job's interval with your idle timeout. If the job runs more often, the service is always on, whatever the config says.
  3. Make a green check mean the thing worked. Ignored monitor traffic, a curl -f against a 202, and a timer that fired all looked fine while backups and services were down. For anything on-demand, check the outcome: the start command's exit code, the last completed snapshot, an actual restore.
  4. Make private the default and public the exception. Bind the proxy to the tailnet address, issue certificates with DNS-01, and make "public" a separate entrypoint that a route has to opt into. A service you forget to think about then stays private.
  5. Tag your own images with the commit, and deploy by committing the new tag. docker ps then tells you exactly what's deployed, git tells you when it changed, and a rollback is a one-line change.

title: Shipping a 2B LLM inside a travel app: what fits on a phone
excerpt: NomadSafe runs Qwen 3.5 on the phone with llama.rn. The 4B model got cut for being too slow, the 2B ships at 1.4 GB, and most of the work was downloads, memory and native crashes rather than prompts.
contentHtml:
The 4B model worked. It was a 3 GB file that needed a phone with 8 GB of RAM. The commit that removed it says why it had to go: "too slow on phones (long waits, hangs)".

NomadSafe is my offline-first travel companion, built with Expo and React Native. It now ships two on-device models, a 0.8B and a 2B, both Qwen 3.5 in GGUF Q4_K_M, run through llama.rn. Choosing the model was the short part. Most of the commits went into getting a 1.4 GB file onto a phone and keeping a native inference context from taking the app down with it.

Why run a model on the phone at all

The app reads things people would rather not send anywhere: Gmail booking confirmations, bank SMS, spends. Google's Limited Use rules for Gmail data are strict, and the app applies the same rule to SMS: raw Gmail and SMS text never leaves the device.

Some tasks are fine to run online. Naming a trip from its destinations is not sensitive. Categorising an expense imported from a bank SMS is. So the app has three AI providers: the user's own API key (called directly from the phone), NomadSafe Cloud for Pro users, and the on-device model. The interesting question is which tasks may use which.

The constraints

These are the ones that shaped the code:

  • RAM. A loaded 2B model plus its KV cache costs a lot of memory, and Android kills background apps by memory use. A model held while backgrounded makes NomadSafe the first app to go.
  • Storage. Travellers' phones are full of photos, and a model download shouldn't be the thing that fills the disk.
  • Network. Downloads start on hotel Wi-Fi and get interrupted by checkout, airplane mode, or the OS killing the app.
  • Native failures. A bad OpenCL driver or a context freed mid-completion is a native crash. JavaScript try/catch never sees it; the app just disappears.

Picking the model: RAM first, then storage

Here are the three models the app has offered, all Q4_K_M quantisation:

Model

Display name

File size

Min RAM

Status

Qwen 3.5 0.8B

NomadBase

579,615,840 bytes (~580 MB)

3 GB

Shipping

Qwen 3.5 2B

NomadPro

1,396,198,496 bytes (~1.4 GB)

4 GB

Shipping

Qwen 3.5 4B

(was NomadPro)

3,013,027,808 bytes (~3.0 GB)

8 GB

Dropped: too slow

I don't have clean tokens-per-second numbers to share yet. What the history does show is the 4B getting cut five days after automatic model selection shipped, with a cleanup path that deletes it from devices that already had it and cancels any 4B download still in flight.

The selection is one pure function in modelCatalog.ts, with no React Native imports, so the Node test suite bundles it directly:

export function pickModelForDevice({ totalRamGb, freeBytes, presentBytes }: DeviceProfileInput): ModelPick {
  const eligible = AI_MODELS.filter((m) => totalRamGb >= m.minRamGb);
  if (eligible.length === 0) return { model: null, reason: "unsupportedDevice", downgraded: false };

  const storageKnown = freeBytes !== null && Number.isFinite(freeBytes) && freeBytes > 0;
  for (let i = eligible.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    const model = eligible[i];
    const credit = Math.min(presentBytes?.[model.id] ?? 0, model.sizeBytes);
    if (!storageKnown || (freeBytes as number) + credit >= model.sizeBytes + STORAGE_HEADROOM_BYTES) {
      return { model, reason: "ok", downgraded: i !== eligible.length - 1 };
    }
  }
  return { model: null, reason: "insufficientStorage", downgraded: false };
}

RAM decides the ceiling, then storage walks it down one tier at a time. STORAGE_HEADROOM_BYTES is 1 GB: the model only counts as fitting if a gigabyte is still free after it lands.

Three details in that function are easy to miss:

  1. Credit bytes already on disk. A finished 1.4 GB download reduces free space by 1.4 GB. Without presentBytes, the 2B no longer "fits" on the next launch and the picker would downgrade a phone that already has it. The test comment puts it plainly: "A finished download must not push itself out on the next launch."
  2. Unknown storage means "assume it fits". If free space comes back as null, 0 or NaN, the picker keeps the RAM tier. Refusing to download on bad telemetry is worse than an insufficientSpace failure from the downloader, which the app handles anyway.
  3. Round RAM to the marketed size. The OS always reports less than the box says, so nominalRamGb does Math.ceil(totalBytes / GB - 0.05); the tests map a reported 7.4 GB to 8 and 3.6 GB to 4. Without it, a 4 GB phone reporting 3.6 GB would get the 0.8B.

The provisioner adds one more rule on top: never trade a verified model for a smaller one just because storage got tight later. If you already have the 2B and fill your phone with photos, you keep the 2B.

Model size on disk isn't the whole memory bill. The context window is sized at load time from available memory: 4,096 tokens when the OS reports under 1,200 MB of available memory (or can't say), up to 8,192 for the 0.8B and 12,288 for the 2B when more than 2,800 MB is available. On iOS, production builds also add the increased-memory-limit and extended-virtual-addressing entitlements that llama.rn needs.

Routing by privacy class, not by quality

The obvious way to route AI tasks is by quality: try the best model, fall back to worse ones. That's what NomadSafe does for chat. For anything touching Gmail or SMS text, it's the wrong question. The rule lives in one table in policy.ts:

const ONLINE_FIRST = ["byok", "cloud", "local"] as const satisfies readonly AiProvider[];

export const AI_TASK_ROUTES: Record<AiTask, readonly AiProvider[]> = {
  chat: ONLINE_FIRST,
  tripBudget: ONLINE_FIRST,
  tripName: ONLINE_FIRST,
  // Only the transcript text goes online, never audio.
  voiceExpense: ONLINE_FIRST,
  // Refine only cleans up Gmail imports, and Gmail text must stay on the phone.
  itinerary: ["local"],
  // Imports carry raw Gmail/SMS text, which must never leave the device.
  expenseCategory: ["local"],
  // Yes/no on unsure Gmail finds: reads the email text.
  emailCheck: ["local"],
  // Only the text read on the phone goes online, never the photo.
  receiptItems: ["byok", "cloud"],
};

Each task's route is the list of providers it may use, in order. A provider that isn't set up, is offline or fails falls through to the next. A provider that isn't in the list can never be used, whatever the user's settings say.

User preference sits on top of the table without being able to break it. providerOrder moves the user's pick to the front only if it's on the task's route. Picking "on-device" with a model ready means nothing goes online at all. Picking "cloud" for expenseCategory is silently ignored, and the test pins that:

assert.deepEqual(policy.providerOrder("expenseCategory", { ...all, preferred: "cloud" }), ["local"]);

The local-only tasks have to cope with the model not being there yet. categorizeExpense and checkEmail return null instead of throwing when no model is ready; for categories, the caller falls back to a heuristic. An import never waits on a 1.4 GB download.

receiptItems is the mirror image: it has no on-device route at all. Privacy is handled there by what's sent (the text read on the phone, never the photo), not by where it runs.

Getting 1.4 GB onto a phone

On Android, the first version downloaded with expo-file-system into the cache directory, writing in place. Two problems: Android may purge the cache directory under storage pressure, and a killed download left a partial file with the final name. The migration code still carries a scar from it: a legacy cache file counts as complete only if it's at least 80% of the expected size, and is deleted otherwise.

The second version (commit 9931864) wrote to a .part file in the documents directory, checked HTTP status and exact size before renaming, and only auto-resumed on Wi-Fi. That's still the iOS path today.

On Android, I stopped downloading from JavaScript entirely. Commit 4049663 added a small Expo native module, expo-system-downloader, that wraps the system DownloadManager. The OS owns the download, so it survives the app being killed and the phone rebooting, and shows its own progress notification. The core is about ten lines of Kotlin:

Function("enqueue") { url: String, fileName: String, title: String, description: String, wifiOnly: Boolean ->
  val target = File(modelsDir(), fileName)
  if (target.exists()) target.delete()
  val request = DownloadManager.Request(Uri.parse(url))
    .setTitle(title)
    .setDescription(description)
    .setNotificationVisibility(DownloadManager.Request.VISIBILITY_VISIBLE)
    .setDestinationUri(Uri.fromFile(target))
    .setAllowedOverMetered(!wifiOnly)
    .setAllowedOverRoaming(!wifiOnly)
  manager.enqueue(request).toString()
}

Files land in the app-specific external directory, which needs no storage permission and is removed on uninstall. The same module exposes query, fileSize, deleteFile and sha256, which streams the file through MessageDigest in 1 MiB chunks so JavaScript never touches 1.4 GB of bytes.

DownloadManager has sharp edges, and these are the ones that cost me time:

  • remove() deletes the file. That holds even after a successful download. Both the Kotlin module and the provisioner carry a comment about it: on success, clear the stored download id, never remove the entry.
  • You can't relax a queued request. When the user taps "Use mobile data", the Wi-Fi-only request has to be removed and re-enqueued. Mobile-data consent then resets after that one download.
  • Entries vanish. A user can clear the download from the Downloads app. query returns missing, and the provisioner re-enqueues once.
  • getExternalFilesDir returns null while shared storage is unavailable. That surfaces as a storageUnavailable error rather than a crash.

Verification is exact size and then SHA-256 against a hash pinned in the catalog, alongside a pinned Hugging Face revision. iOS has no streaming native hash in the app yet, so on iOS the check is exact size only. A file that fails verification is deleted, and transient failures (incomplete, corrupt, network, unknown) get two silent retries before the user sees an error card. That retry limit came from a bug where a truncated file left a persisted incomplete error that blocked re-download forever.

The whole thing is driven by one idempotent function, ensureProvisioned(). Launch, network changes, the settings toggle, the background task and the UI all call it; concurrent calls coalesce into one extra pass. It polls DownloadManager every 1.5 s only while a screen showing progress is mounted and the app is in the foreground. A background task with a 15-minute minimum interval is registered only while a download is pending, so the OS stops waking the app once the model is ready.

Keeping the native context from crashing the app

Before 9931864, model loading had a de-duplication guard: an in-flight load was shared if a second caller asked for the same model with the same context size. The comment explained why it existed: two concurrent initLlama calls for the same model fail natively.

The hole was the "same context size" part. A request needing a larger window started a fresh load, and that load began by releasing the active context, whether or not a completion was still streaming from it. release() itself freed the context immediately too. Freeing native memory under a running completion is not an exception you can catch. Two overlapping loads could also each create a context with only the last one stored, which is the "leaked contexts" the fix commit mentions.

The fix was to stop coordinating and serialise everything. Every load, completion and release goes through one promise chain:

function enqueue<T>(task: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  const run = queueTail.then(task);
  queueTail = run.then(() => undefined, () => undefined);
  return run;
}

async release(): Promise<void> {
  if (pendingJobs > 0) {
    releaseRequested = true; // runs when the queue drains
    return;
  }
  await enqueue(releaseContext);
}

That turns release() into a request rather than a command, so any screen can call it at any time. A loaded context is reused if it's big enough for the next prompt; otherwise it's released and reloaded inside the same queue slot, so nothing else can touch it in between.

With release safe to call, unloading became a policy question. A loaded model holds gigabytes, so NomadSafe lets go of it aggressively (commit 247db77 added the first two):

  • Leaving the AI tab: releaseAfter(20_000). When the phone model is the source, the tab preloads it on focus, and on blur asks for release 20 s after the current work finishes. Coming back within 20 s reuses the warm context.
  • Backgrounding: release immediately (deferred if a completion is running).
  • iOS memory warning: release. React Native doesn't forward Android's onTrimMemory, so there's no equivalent there.
  • Otherwise idle: release after 3 minutes with no model work.

GPU offload with a crash-loop guard

On iOS, llama.rn offloads all layers to Metal, falling back to CPU if allocation fails. On Android the app was CPU-only until 4049663 added OpenCL offload. GPU drivers vary a lot across Android vendors, and a broken one doesn't throw: it crashes the process. Do that during model load and the app crashes every time the user opens the AI tab.

The pattern I used is a write-ahead flag in MMKV, which survives a process crash:

async function initAndroidGpu(model: AiModel, params: LoadParams) {
  if (storage.getBoolean(GPU_DISABLED_KEY)) return null;
  storage.set(GPU_ATTEMPT_KEY, model.id);
  try {
    const context = await initLlama({ ...params, n_gpu_layers: 99, flash_attn_type: "auto" });
    if (storage.getString(GPU_VERIFIED_KEY) !== model.id) {
      await context.completion({ prompt: "Hi", n_predict: 1, temperature: 0 });
      storage.set(GPU_VERIFIED_KEY, model.id);
    }
    storage.remove(GPU_ATTEMPT_KEY);
    return context;
  } catch (err) {
    storage.remove(GPU_ATTEMPT_KEY);
    storage.set(GPU_DISABLED_KEY, true);
    return null; // caller loads on CPU (trimmed: missing-file errors rethrow, a half-made context is released)
  }
}

And at module load, before anything else:

if (Platform.OS === "android" && storage.getString(GPU_ATTEMPT_KEY)) {
  storage.set(GPU_DISABLED_KEY, true);
  storage.remove(GPU_ATTEMPT_KEY);
}

If the flag is still there at launch, the last GPU attempt never got to clear it, so it died natively. GPU is disabled for good on that device and the user gets one crash, not a loop. The 1-token probe exists because a successful load doesn't prove the GPU can run a completion. It runs once per model, so normal loads don't pay for it.

The CPU path passes no_gpu_devices: true, which keeps OpenCL uninitialised entirely, so a broken driver can't crash the fallback either. It then retries once without flash attention if the first CPU load fails. Every load logs whether it landed on GPU and, if not, llama.rn's reasonNoGPU.

What I'd tell you to steal

Make model selection a pure function of RAM, free storage and bytes present

Keep it out of React Native so you can unit test the boundaries: 2.9 GB, 3 GB, 3.9 GB, 4 GB, exactly-fits storage, unknown storage. Round reported RAM up to the marketed size, keep a storage headroom, and credit files already on disk or your own download will evict itself.

Route by what the input contains, then by quality

Put the rule in one table where a missing provider means "never", and write a test that a user preference can't override it. Design those private-only tasks to return null and fall back to a heuristic, so the feature works before the model arrives.

Use a write-ahead flag for anything that can crash natively

Set it before the risky call, clear it after a probe succeeds, and check it at startup. It costs two key-value writes and turns a crash loop into a single crash. The same trick works for any native module that may crash on a specific driver.

Serialise native calls through one queue

Make release a request, not a command. Once release() is safe from anywhere, you can unload aggressively (20 s off-screen, on background) without auditing every caller.

On Android, let the OS download large files

DownloadManager survives process death and reboots, and handles Wi-Fi-only for you. Verify by exact size and a pinned hash, and never call remove() on a finished entry.

Model size ended up being the easy decision. A 2B model at 4-bit is about as large as I'd ship to a phone today, and the rest of the work was making a 1.4 GB native dependency behave like any other part of the app.

title: Bending light at 120 Hz: rebuilding Liquid Glass on Android
excerpt: How react-native-liquid-tabs fakes a refracting glass droplet on Android with one Skia shader, a blur cropped to the bar at quarter size, and springs that behave the same at 60 and 120 Hz.
contentHtml:
At 120 Hz you get 8.3 ms per frame. With a stock full-screen blur behind it, a glass tab bar on Android spent about 11 ms on every frame of a drag, and 48% of those frames janked. Cropping the blur took drag frames to about 8 ms and jank to 4%.

That bar is now react-native-liquid-tabs, the iOS 26 Liquid Glass tab bar rebuilt for Android. Most of what it took is reusable elsewhere: refraction faked with a distance field, blur cropped to what you need, 120 Hz requested only while something moves, and springs that don't care about the refresh rate.

What I was copying

On iOS 26 the selected tab is a drop of glass. Press the bar and the drop lifts, swells, and follows your finger. The icons under it are magnified and bent, the edges fringe with colour, and when you let go it lands on a tab and spreads back into the pill.

On iOS I don't rebuild any of it: LiquidTabs renders Expo Router's NativeTabs, so iOS gets the real system bar. Everything below is Android.

The constraints:

  • React Native, Reanimated 4 and Skia, plus a small Kotlin module for what JS can't do.
  • A real blur of the content behind the bar. RenderEffect blur needs Android 12 (API 31); older devices get tinted glass without the blur.
  • 120 Hz on adaptive screens while the drop moves, and zero work while it's idle.
  • React must not render during a drag. Everything runs on the UI thread; the only JS hops are waking the animation and the final tab switch.

Physics and look were tuned frame by frame against iOS 26 screen recordings, hence the oddly specific constants.

One frame, end to end

The bar is three layers: a native blur view at the bottom, a Skia canvas in the middle that draws the icons and the drop, and a row of invisible tab cells on top that take the touches and carry the accessibility roles.

The Skia layer never reads the blur. It only paints over it, which matters later.

Blur only what's behind you

A general-purpose Android blur view, like the BlurView library that expo-blur wraps, blurs its whole target at full resolution. For a 64 dp bar over a full-screen feed, that means blurring the entire screen every frame to show a strip at the bottom. At 60 Hz that fits. At 120 Hz it doesn't.

The fix has two halves. First, BlurTarget (LiquidBlurTargetView.kt) records its children into a RenderNode inside dispatchDraw, then draws that node normally. Recording is cheap (a display list, not pixels), and any blur view can replay it.

Second, the glass view (LiquidBlurView.kt) replays only the part of that node behind itself, at a quarter of the size, and blurs that:

val pad = blurRadius * 2f                       // the blur reaches this far; include it
val smallWidth = ceil((width + pad * 2f) / SCALE).toInt()   // SCALE = 4
val smallHeight = ceil((height + pad * 2f) / SCALE).toInt()
blurNode.setPosition(0, 0, smallWidth, smallHeight)
val recording = blurNode.beginRecording(smallWidth, smallHeight)
recording.scale(1f / SCALE, 1f / SCALE)
recording.translate(pad - lastLeft, pad - lastTop) // our offset inside the target
rootView?.background?.draw(recording)
recording.drawRenderNode(sourceNode)              // replay, cropped by the node's bounds
blurNode.endRecording()
blurNode.setRenderEffect(RenderEffect.createBlurEffect(r / SCALE, r / SCALE, CLAMP))

canvas.save()
canvas.translate(-pad, -pad)
canvas.scale(SCALE, SCALE)                        // back to full size
canvas.drawRenderNode(blurNode)
canvas.restore()
canvas.drawRect(0f, 0f, width.toFloat(), height.toFloat(), noisePaint(context))

(Trimmed: the real code only rebuilds the RenderEffect when the radius changes.)

Three things make this work:

  • The pad. A blur at the edge of the crop needs pixels from outside it, so the crop extends by twice the radius on every side. Without it the edges of the bar would blur against clamped edge pixels instead of their real neighbours.
  • Quarter size. A 4x downscale is 1/16 of the pixels, and the blur radius shrinks by 4 too. A blur throws away high frequencies anyway, so the upscale costs nothing you can see.
  • Noise. Upscaled blur can band on smooth gradients. A faint tiled blue-noise texture (from BlurView, at alpha 38/255) breaks the bands up and reads as frosted glass.

Content changes reach the blur through the target's RenderNode on their own, so an OnPreDrawListener only invalidates the view when its offset inside the target changes.

Blur strategy

Drag frame time

Janky frames

Whole target, full size

~11 ms

48%

Bar + pad, 1/4 size

~8 ms

4%

The same controller is about 160 lines of Java, and it drops into expo-blur too. I carry it as a dependency patch (CroppedBlurController) in another app, installed in place of BlurView's stock controller on API 31+. If you use expo-blur over scrolling content on Android, that patch is the easiest thing here to try first.

Faking refraction with a distance field

Real refraction follows Snell's law through a 3D surface. You don't need that to fool an eye at 120 Hz. For every pixel inside the drop, the shader answers one question: which point of the unbent image should this pixel show? Refraction becomes a UV offset.

To decide the offset you need two things at every pixel: how far it is from the rim, and which way the rim faces. A signed distance field gives you both. sdCapsule returns a negative distance inside the capsule, zero on the rim, positive outside. The rim's direction (the normal) is the gradient of that distance, which you get numerically by sampling it 0.75 dp either side on each axis. That's central differences, and it works for any shape without deriving a normal by hand.

Trimmed from the LENS shader in src/GlassTabBar.tsx:

float2 rel = p - center;                 // pixel relative to the drop's centre, in dp
float d = sdCapsule(rel, halfSize);      // < 0 inside, 0 on the rim
if (d > 1.5) return base;                // outside the drop: draw unbent

// Normal = gradient of the distance, by central differences
float e = 0.75;
float2 n = normalize(float2(
  sdCapsule(rel + float2(e, 0.0), halfSize) - sdCapsule(rel - float2(e, 0.0), halfSize),
  sdCapsule(rel + float2(0.0, e), halfSize) - sdCapsule(rel - float2(0.0, e), halfSize)) + 0.00001);

// 1. Magnify: read nearer the centre than we are
float2 q = center + rel / (1.0 + magnify * lift);

// 2. Rim bend: in the outer band, read further out along the normal
float edge = 1.0 - clamp(-d / band, 0.0, 1.0);   // 0 deep inside, 1 on the rim
float bend = edge * edge;
float2 src = q + n * bend * (distortion + motion * 6.0) * lift;

// 3. Colour split: red and blue read from slightly different points
float split = (chroma * (1.0 + 0.2 * ends) + motion * 1.5) * bend * lift;
half r = content(src + n * split).r;
half4 g = content(src);
half b = content(src - n * split).b;

Magnification. Dividing the offset from the centre by 1 + 0.18 * lift means each pixel reads from a point closer to the centre than itself. Content therefore looks about 1.18x larger at full lift, on top of the 5% swell the whole bar gets while pressed. Every term is scaled by lift (0 to 1 as the drop pops up), so the effects fade in together.

Rim bend. band is 60% of the drop's half-height. Inside that band, edge rises from 0 to 1 toward the rim, and squaring it keeps the middle flat and pushes the curve into the last few dp, as a thick glass edge does. The push follows the outward normal, so the flat top and bottom "look outward": they show what's beyond them and pull the bar's own rim inward, so the bar reads thinner through the drop. distortion is 9 dp at the 402 dp reference width, and motion (speed scaled to 0..1, saturating at 2.2 dp/ms) adds up to 6 dp more while it moves.

End caps. The rounded ends get a different lens: a radial pull toward each cap's centre that grows with distance, up to 32%. It smears whatever sits under the tip into a bright, round blob.

Chromatic split. Red and blue sample a little either side of green along the normal, only in the rim band, and further apart when moving.

After the refraction come three cheap touches that sell it as glass:

  • pastBar. When the rim bend looks past the bar's edge, the sample lands where the shader has no blur to show, since it can't read the native view below. It paints the page colour there instead, which is what the backgroundColor prop is for.
  • A rim light. A hairline at d ≈ 0, brightened where the normal faces a fixed key light direction, plus a faint Fresnel glow just inside it.
  • An opacity ramp. The glass becomes fully opaque early in the lift and ignores spring overshoot, so the unbent icons never show through as a ghost copy.

One shaded rect per frame

The obvious way to draw a tab bar in Skia is to draw each icon path and label every frame. But the shader needs the row as something it can sample at arbitrary points, three times per pixel, and a list of draw calls isn't that.

Instead, both icon rows (plain and selected, with the bar's rim stroke) are rendered once with drawAsImage into device-pixel images. Per frame the canvas is a single <Fill> with the LENS shader, and those two images are its child shaders. The content() function inside the shader chooses between them: the selected row inside the drop and under the resting tab, the plain row elsewhere. A frame is one rect, a few texture reads per pixel, and a useDerivedValue that recomputes the uniforms on the UI thread.

The images only rebuild when something visible changes. The cache key is built from the items' content rather than the array identity, because callers often rebuild items every render.

One gotcha: on a cold start Android can drop the canvas's first frame because its surface isn't attached yet, and an idle bar never draws again, so it stays empty until touched. The fix is blunt: bump a repaint shared value 100 ms and 500 ms after the images are ready.

Springs that don't care about the refresh rate

The drop follows its goal (the finger's travel, or a tab) through an underdamped spring. The obvious integration is one Euler step per frame with dt from the frame callback. That gives a different trajectory at 60 Hz than at 120 Hz, and a dropped frame becomes one giant step that can overshoot wildly.

So the frame callback slices whatever time passed into equal sub-steps of at most 4 ms:

const dt = Math.min(48, info.timeSincePreviousFrame ?? 16); // cap a long stall
const steps = Math.ceil(dt / STEP_MS);                       // STEP_MS = 4
const h = dt / steps;
for (let i = 0; i < steps; i++) {
  const before = g - p;
  const past = p < min || p > max;           // swung past the first or last tab
  const omega = past ? END_OMEGA : FOLLOW_OMEGA;
  const zeta = past ? END_ZETA : FOLLOW_ZETA;
  v += (omega * omega * before - 2 * zeta * omega * v) * h;
  p += v * h;                                 // velocity first: semi-implicit Euler
  if (!held && before * (g - p) < 0) {        // a landing never overshoots its tab
    p = g;
    v = 0;
  }
}

That's three sub-steps per frame at 120 Hz and five at 60 Hz, a few multiplications each. In return you get the same motion on every device and through hitches. Updating velocity before position (semi-implicit Euler) keeps the spring stable where plain Euler slowly gains energy.

The constants, with units of dp and milliseconds:

Spring

ω (1/ms)

ζ

What it does

Follow

0.027

0.7

Trails a moving finger by 2ζ/ω ≈ 52 ms

End

0.08

0.5

Stiffer, bouncier past the end tabs (max 5 dp)

Squash

0.05

1.0

Flattens to bar height, ~9% wider, as speed rises

Bulge

0.005

0.7

After slowing: ~12% taller, ~7% narrower, peaking ~0.22 s

The 2ζ/ω lag is a handy number. A damped spring chasing a target at constant speed settles a fixed 2ζ/ω behind it (set acceleration to zero in the spring equation and solve), so you can tune how far behind the finger it feels directly.

The squash and bulge only run while a finger drags and reduced motion is off. Deceleration kicks the bulge spring (each sub-step where speed dropped adds velocity to it), which is why the drop goes tall right after you stop.

Landing has one guard worth copying: once released, the drop snaps to its tab the moment it would cross it, so a tap on the last tab can't carry it past the bar's end.

120 Hz only while something moves

Android adaptive displays often idle at 60 Hz or lower. A window can ask for more through preferredRefreshRate. The module picks the display's top supported mode while the drop moves and hands the choice back by setting 0:

Function("setHighFrameRate") { high: Boolean ->
  val activity = appContext.currentActivity ?: return@Function
  activity.runOnUiThread {
    val window = activity.window ?: return@runOnUiThread
    val display = activity.display          // windowManager.defaultDisplay below API 30
    val top = display?.supportedModes?.maxOfOrNull { it.refreshRate } ?: 0f
    val attrs = window.attributes
    val wanted = if (high) top else 0f
    if (attrs.preferredRefreshRate != wanted) {
      attrs.preferredRefreshRate = wanted
      window.attributes = attrs
    }
    // API 35+: opt out of frame-rate power savings while high
    if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 35) window.setFrameRatePowerSavingsBalanced(!high)
  }
}

The other half is stopping work. The useFrameCallback is created inactive. A press or tab change sets a liquidRunning flag on the UI thread, then activates the callback and requests 120 Hz. Once every spring is at rest, the callback clears the flag and schedules stopLiquid on the JS thread, which deactivates the callback and releases the refresh rate.

There's a race: the stop runs a little later, and a new press may have restarted the drop in between. Every caller sets liquidRunning on the UI thread first, so stopLiquid checks it and backs off if set. An idle bar runs no frame callback and makes no refresh-rate request, and its glass is a single blur pass; the lighter "pressed" blur layer is only mounted while the bar is held.

Limits

  • The blur needs Android 12. Below that the bar draws on tinted glass with the same lens.
  • The glass must sit outside the BlurTarget it blurs; a view can't blur a recording of itself. The Kotlin side detects this and logs a warning instead of recursing.

What I'd tell you to steal

Crop and shrink your blurs. Blur only the view's own rect plus twice the radius, at quarter size, and add noise. It looks the same and costs a fraction. Measure against your real budget (8.3 ms at 120 Hz), not "feels fine at 60".

Treat refraction as choosing where to sample. An SDF gives you depth and, through central differences, a normal for any shape. Scale toward the centre to magnify, push along the normal near the edge to bend, split R and B along the same normal for dispersion.

Integrate springs in small sub-steps. Clamp dt, cut it into steps of at most 4 ms, update velocity before position. Motion then matches across 60, 90 and 120 Hz and survives dropped frames.

Tie high refresh rate to motion. Request the display's top mode when the animation starts, release it in the same place you stop your frame loop, and guard the stop against a restart that raced it.

Pre-render whatever doesn't change per frame. Draw static content once into an image and let one shader do the per-frame work.

The library is react-native-liquid-tabs on npm, MIT licensed, with Expo Router and React Navigation examples in the repo.

title: The workaround was the leak: chasing 1.4 GB of GPU memory in React Native Skia
excerpt: Three animated path canvases in react-native-skia v3 were holding 1.4 GB of GPU memory on a Samsung phone. The cause turned out to be my own fix for an Adreno crash, and the real fix was one Dawn feature flag.
contentHtml:
Three animated <Canvas> views, each drawing a few dashed lines, were using 1,366 MB of GPU memory on a Samsung Galaxy SM-S948B, and the number was still going up after 90 seconds. On an iPhone, the whole app's memory footprint on the same screen stayed around 107 MB. In a real app with several path canvases on one screen I had seen 2.1 GB, then swap, then a low-memory kill.

This is how I tracked that down in react-native-skia v3. Most of what I measured was correct. The assumption underneath it was wrong, and it was mine.

It started with a crash

React Native Skia v3 renders with Skia's Graphite backend. On Android, Graphite talks to Dawn (Chrome's WebGPU implementation), Dawn talks to Vulkan, and Vulkan talks to the vendor driver, here Qualcomm's Adreno.

As soon as a canvas drew animated stroked paths, or one large filled path, the app died within about a second:

F DEBUG   : signal 11 (SIGSEGV), code 1 (SEGV_MAPERR), fault addr 0x0000000000000008 (read)
F DEBUG   : Cause: null pointer dereference
  #02 pc 00000000001afad8  /vendor/lib64/hw/vulkan.adreno.so (qglinternal::vkCreateFramebuffer(...)+248)

Graphite draws paths into a 4x multisampled (MSAA) render pass by default. Turning that off made the crash go away completely, so that became the workaround. It had first gone into a production app on 3.0.1, on the same phone model, and it was one line in RNDawnContext.h:

#ifdef __ANDROID__
    // Adreno's Vulkan driver crashes in vkCreateFramebuffer when Graphite
    // opens the multisampled render pass it uses for large and stroked paths.
    ctxOptions.fInternalMultisampleCount = skgpu::graphite::SampleCount::k1;
#endif

The crash stopped, the paths rendered, and some time later the memory reports started.

A cross-check on the rows

My sampler had a bug in its first version. It pulled the row out of the dumpsys text, and the match hit EGL mtrack first, because "EGL mtrack" contains "GL mtrack". Every early CSV has a column called gl_mtrack_mb that is actually EGL mtrack. You can see it in the data: across the children, clip and layer scenarios that column reads 157.2 MB every time, while the Graphics total moves between 175 and 253 MB.

The fix is to match on fields, not substrings:

mem=$("$ADB" -s "$SERIAL" shell dumpsys meminfo $PKG)
gl=$(echo "$mem" | awk '$1=="GL" && $2=="mtrack" {print $3; exit}')
gfx=$(echo "$mem" | awk '/Graphics:/ {print $2; exit}')
pss=$(echo "$mem" | awk '/TOTAL PSS:/ {print $3; exit}')

The bug didn't change any conclusion, because I judged those early runs by the Graphics total, which I was also logging. That is the reason to log more than one row.

A few other habits from scripts/android-run.sh that saved me from bad samples:

  • Refuse to start if the screen is off or the keyguard is showing.
  • Launch the scenario with am start -W -S, which force-stops the app first, so every run starts cold.
  • Record whether the app was focused at each sample. In one 10-minute run, the sample at 61 s reads 0.0 MB with focused=0. Without that column it would look like the GPU released everything.

A repro small enough to be believed

The production app was too big to reason about, so I built a separate Expo app: SDK 57, React Native 0.86, Reanimated 4.5, react-native-skia 3.0.8. Every scenario is a deep link, so a script can run it with no tapping:

skiarepro://run?s=dashN&n=3              # 3 canvases of animated dashed strokes
skiarepro://run?s=paths                  # one big rotating self-intersecting path
skiarepro://run?s=idle&n=5               # 5 canvases, uniform-only runtime shaders
skiarepro://run?s=dashN&n=3&budget=32    # same, with a 32 MB recorder budget

The path scenario uses the library the standard way. Paths come from usePathValue driven by a Reanimated clock, and nothing is allocated per frame on the JS side. That matters when you file the issue: "the documented API, used as documented, costs 256 MB per canvas" is hard to argue with.

The repo also holds every raw CSV, the crash tombstone, a pnpm patch to switch between stock and patched builds, and a README note on which CSVs the sampler bug affects.

What Graphite was holding on to

The useful mental model for Graphite's memory is this. Each Recorder owns a resource cache. When a frame is done with a texture or buffer, the resource goes back into the cache as purgeable, ready to be reused. The cache only frees purgeable resources when it goes over its budget, or when someone calls performDeferredCleanup() for resources unused for some period.

React Native Skia creates one Recorder per canvas, in RNSkGraphiteTarget.h. Neither the recorders nor the context set fGpuBudgetInBytes, so each gets Skia's default, kDefaultRecorderBudget, which is 256 MB. Nothing in the library called performDeferredCleanup either.

I added temporary logging of currentBudgetedBytes() after a performDeferredCleanup(5 s) call every 2 seconds. With a 128 MB budget and three dash canvases:

SKMEM recorder 0x…3f30 budgeted 130512KB -> 130512KB purgeable 113007KB max 131072KB

Each recorder sat exactly at its budget, almost all of it purgeable. With the budget at 8 MB, one recorder held 17,504 KB with nothing purgeable. That is what one frame of this path work actually needs: about 17 MB. Everything above that was old frames' resources waiting for a purge that only the budget would trigger. And because each resource had been used within the last few seconds, the time-based cleanup freed almost nothing.

Strictly, this isn't a leak. The cache did what it was configured to do, with a desktop default, once per canvas.

The wrong turn

My own crash issue already said that turning MSAA off is what sends paths down the code path that fills the cache. I had written down the twist and walked past it.

Look at iOS again. Metal, MSAA on, three dash canvases: 104 → 107 MB over 90 seconds. Same recorders, same 256 MB budgets, no growth. The cache budget was real, but it was only being reached because I had moved every path onto a resource-hungry route to avoid a crash I didn't understand. The workaround was the leak.

The real question was why MSAA crashed on Adreno at all. And MSAA is not one switch. On a GPU that advertises VK_EXT_multisampled_render_to_single_sampled, Dawn can expose the MSAARenderToSingleSampled feature. With that feature, Graphite renders multisampled straight into a single-sampled texture and lets the driver handle the sample storage, instead of allocating a separate MSAA attachment and resolving it.

React Native Skia requested that feature in createDawnBackendContext() in RNDawnUtils.h. Leaving out only that feature, with MSAA still on, stopped the crash on both path scenarios.

I opened #4177 with a gate on Qualcomm GPUs and reported the driver crash to Dawn as issue 571594984. Then I reran #4159's scenario with MSAA back on: three animated path canvases stayed flat at about 80 MB on the same Adreno phone, like iOS.

What the validation layers found

My crash issue had listed this as an open item: "Our tombstone has no Vulkan validation output, so we don't know what makes the framebuffer invalid." William ran the Khronos validation layers against the library's example app on a Pixel 8 (Mali-G715), and they answered it. Dawn creates its Vulkan swapchain images without VK_IMAGE_CREATE_MULTISAMPLED_RENDER_TO_SINGLE_SAMPLED_BIT_EXT. The spec requires that flag on every single-sampled attachment of such a pass, so every MSAA pass Graphite draws onto the window violates VUID-VkFramebufferCreateInfo-samples-06881.

That changes the reading of the bug. The root cause isn't in the Adreno driver. It is invalid API usage on every driver that advertises the extension; Mali tolerates it, and Adreno's crash is just how it shows up there. My Qualcomm gate would have hidden the violation on the one GPU where it was visible and left it everywhere else.

I hadn't run them myself, and I should have. On a debuggable Android build the setup is short: package libVkLayer_khronos_validation.so (from the Khronos Vulkan-ValidationLayers releases) into the app's native libraries, then:

adb shell settings put global enable_gpu_debug_layers 1
adb shell settings put global gpu_debug_app com.example.app
adb shell settings put global gpu_debug_layers VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation
# reproduce, read the VUID messages in logcat, then turn it off:
adb shell settings delete global enable_gpu_debug_layers

A VUID turns "the driver crashed" into "this rule in the spec was broken", which upstream can act on. William also opened a Dawn test, google/dawn#88, that runs a 4x pass on a surface texture and fails under backend validation on affected drivers.

The fix

The merged change leaves the feature out on Android entirely:

std::vector<wgpu::FeatureName> features = {
#if !defined(__ANDROID__)
    // Not on Android: Dawn creates its Vulkan swapchain images without
    // VK_IMAGE_CREATE_MULTISAMPLED_RENDER_TO_SINGLE_SAMPLED_BIT_EXT, so every
    // MSAA pass Graphite draws onto the window with this feature violates
    // VUID-VkFramebufferCreateInfo-samples-06881 ...
    // Re-enable once Dawn creates swapchains with the flag or reports which
    // textures cannot take an implicit sample count:
    // https://issues.chromium.org/issues/571594984
    wgpu::FeatureName::MSAARenderToSingleSampled,
#endif
    wgpu::FeatureName::TransientAttachments,

Without the feature, Graphite renders through a transient MSAA attachment and resolves it, the same path it already takes on GPUs without the extension. The diff is twelve added lines in RNDawnUtils.h. William asked for the Android-wide version over my vendor gate, pushed it to my branch, and merged it on 13 October. It shipped in 3.4.2, and #4158 closed with it.

What's still open

  • The budget PR, #4160, is still open, and #4159 with it. With MSAA on, path canvases no longer churn, so the main reason for it is gone. It still matters for apps that keep MSAA off on purpose: in my production app, MSAA on costs a lot more memory on Adreno, roughly 285 MB to 495 MB on the home screen. I told the maintainer I'm happy to close it.
  • #4161, image uploads outliving their images, happens with MSAA on as well. On iOS the repro's images scenario sat at 299 MB after unmount on 3.0.8 and 42 MB with the fixes.
  • I still don't know exactly why the MSAA-off path creates about 17 MB of new resources per frame for a few dashed lines.

What I'd tell you to steal

Measure the right row, and two rows. On Android, GL mtrack is the GPU-cache number. Parse it by field, because "EGL mtrack" contains "GL mtrack". Log Graphics: as well and treat disagreement as a bug in your tooling. Record app focus with every sample.

Bisect memory by scenario, not by hunch. Give each suspect its own deep link and run each for the same time from a cold start. A table of flat lines with one rising line is the strongest evidence you can bring, and once you have the harness, testing a theory like the atlas is one rebuild.

Know how GPU caches are bounded. In Skia Graphite, released resources stay as purgeable until the budget is reached, and the budget is per Recorder, which in React Native Skia means per canvas. Before you call growth a leak, print budgeted and purgeable bytes. If the cache sits at its budget and most of it is purgeable, you have a sizing problem.

Treat your workaround as a suspect. When a fix for one bug changes how the renderer works, the next bug you find may be that fix. Compare against a platform without it; iOS at 107 MB was telling me this from the start.

Give upstream something to run: one app, deep links, scripts, raw CSVs, and PRs that say what was not measured. And when a crash is in a driver, run the validation layers before writing a vendor gate. They may show the bug is in your stack, not theirs.
